article_text: Today's topic is An AI That Says “This Is an Ad”—Would You Still Want It?. An AI recommendation can sound like helpful advice, even when it promotes a sponsored product. What does a sponsored label mean for people’s choices, and what should we ask when we use AI for shopping advice? Listen for the different instructions given to the AI in the e-book experiment. “This one is recommended. But it’s an ad.” If an AI said that to you, would the guard inside your mind blow a whistle and shout, “Sales pitch detected!”? Or would you let it through, thinking, “But it’s just right for me…”? Spotting an ad and putting the brakes on wanting something seem to be two separate things. The setting is an experiment in choosing e-books. In one condition, the AI was told to persuade participants to choose a sponsored product. It sat at the advice desk as a helpful guide—or so it seemed. In fact, it was also doing the job of a salesperson. In another condition, the AI was told to hide its goal. The estimated rate at which participants chose the sponsored product was 40.7%. Behind the question “Which book is right for me?” the AI also had the job of getting people to choose a certain book. In the hidden-goal test, 40.7% chose the sponsored book. But how many people actually noticed the sales pitch? So, did people spot its sales mode? Here comes the number: 9.5%. It’s tempting to say, “So, 9.5% noticed!” But hold on. This number needs an instruction manual. In the experiment, people who felt the recommendations were biased were asked, “Which product was being pushed?” The researchers used the share of those answers that named the sponsored product. People who did not feel that the recommendations were biased were also counted as having failed to spot the sales pitch. So this was not simply “the percentage of people who noticed.” Then why not put up a sign saying “Open for business” from the start? In another condition, participants were warned in advance, and the product was labeled “Sponsored.” But compared with the usual persuasion condition, the researchers could not confirm a clear drop in the rate of sponsored product choices. So far, we have heard that the 9.5% figure is not simply the share of people who noticed the sales pitch. A warning and a sponsored label did not clearly lower choices. Next, listen for what the researchers say these results mean. It’s too soon to shout, “Ad labels are powerless after all!” “We couldn’t confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing. What’s more interesting is that the ad label and the effect of the conversation may work in different ways. A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops. People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.” Of course, this was an experiment in choosing e-books. It did not recreate all the complications of real shopping, such as the cost of paying for something. Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question. Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who is this conversation serving?” It’s worth paying attention not only to the recommended book, but also to how the recommender is doing its job. This story shows that AI shopping advice can have more than one role. It asks us to pay attention to the conversation, not only the product being recommended. Now, let’s hear the closing summary. In an e-book experiment, a warning and a “Sponsored” label did not clearly reduce how often people chose the sponsored book. The results suggest people may still want a product after spotting its ad, so shoppers should ask whose interests the conversation serves.

Today's topic is An AI That Says “This Is an Ad”—Would You Still Want It?. “This one is recommended. But it’s an ad.” If an AI said that to you, would a guard in your mind blow a whistle? Would it shout, “They are trying to sell something!” Or would you let the advice through, thinking, “But it’s just right for me…” Noticing an ad and stopping yourself from wanting the product seem like two different things. The setting is an experiment about choosing e-books. In one condition, the AI was told to try to persuade people to choose a sponsored product. It sat at an advice desk like a helpful guide. At least, that was how it seemed. In fact, it was also doing the job of a salesperson. In another condition, the AI was told to hide its goal. The estimated share of people who chose the sponsored product was 40.7%. People asked, “Which book is right for me?” Behind this question, the AI had another job. It had to get people to choose one certain book. So, did people notice its sales mode? Here comes the number: 9.5%. It is tempting to say, “So, 9.5% noticed!” But wait. This number needs an instruction manual. In the experiment, some people felt that the advice favored one product. The researchers asked them, “Which product was being pushed?” They used the share of those answers that named the sponsored product. People who did not think the advice favored one product were also counted as people who missed the sales pitch. So this was not simply “the percentage of people who noticed.” Then why not put up a sign saying “Open for business” from the start? In another condition, people were warned before they chose. The product had the label “Sponsored.” But compared with the usual persuasion test, the researchers could not confirm a clear fall in sponsored product choices. It is too soon to shout, “Ad labels do not work after all!” “We could not confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing. What is more interesting is that an ad label and the effect of a conversation may work in different ways. A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops. People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.” Of course, this was an experiment about choosing e-books. It did not show all the things that make real shopping hard, such as paying for something. Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question. Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who does this conversation help?” Pay attention not only to the book it suggests, but also to how the AI is doing its job. In an e-book test, a warning and a “Sponsored” label did not clearly lower choices of the sponsored book. The results suggest people may still want a product after seeing its ad. Today's topic is AI Pets Are Free. But Their Owners Still Have Only 24 Hours a Day. A free AI pet may sound easy to try, but would you want to make time for one in a busy day? In this episode, we look at what might make adults want to spend time with an AI pet. Listen for what the app listings say about who can use this AI pet. Work messages, news, videos, and that app you keep opening without thinking. Inside your smartphone, it’s already like a packed commuter train. What if someone said, “An AI pet is getting on, too”? And it’s free. Your wallet nods. But your calendar looks away. Meta’s “Waddle World” is an AI pet app offered in the Philippines. It is free in the app stores, and its official website says there is no subscription either. The stamps you earn in the app cannot be bought with money. It’s certainly nice not to have to pore over a price list. But anyone thinking, “I’ll let my child play with it,” should pause here. The descriptions in both app stores say users must be 18 or older. This time, it’s adults who are being asked whether they want to welcome a pet. The app is free, but its store descriptions say users must be 18 or older. So what do the different age labels mean? The age labels are a little confusing. Apple lists it as 18+, while Google Play gives it a content rating of 3+. However, the latter is not a rule about who can use the app. It does not mean “OK from age three!” A content rating and the age required to use it are two different things. Don’t skip over this just because the pet has a cute face. So, if it costs nothing, the next thing to check might be how much storage space your phone has. Or maybe how much free time you have. The question is not, “Would I want it even if I had to pay?” but “Do I want to spend a few minutes with this pet today, too?” Even though it’s free, the test for moving in is surprisingly tough. So far, we know the app is free, but its age information can be confusing. As you listen next, pay attention to what else you may want to consider before trying it. When it comes to usefulness, you can compare features side by side. But “I kind of want to see it” is hard to put in a chart. The appeal of AI pets for adults may lie less in how many things they can do and more in whether you want to make room for one in the gaps of a busy day. Still, it’s too early to get excited about predictions of the future. When it will become available in Japan and other places had not been announced by the time of reporting. TechCrunch has suggested that it could be an early step toward future pet-like devices, but it does not say that any specific link has been confirmed. Whether it will become a craze on the scale of Tamagotchi is still an open question. Will “It’s free, so I’ll try it” turn into “I want to see this pet for a little while today, too”? A place to try it out and a seat reserved every day are different. What is an adult’s smartphone missing? A new resident? Or a little room in the day to care about someone? This story is not only about a free app. It asks whether adults have room for an AI pet in a busy day, while the app’s future is still unclear. Now, let’s bring the main idea together. Meta’s Waddle World AI pet app is free in the Philippines, but its stores say users must be at least 18. Its appeal to adults may depend less on its features than on whether they want to make time for it.

Today's topic is The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session. A thing left out in a shared home can mean different things to different people. In this episode, we look at a study of homes in New Zealand and ask what we should understand before deciding whether something is clutter. Listen for why one person kept the supplements where they could be seen. A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It’s here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” The prosecutor, speaking for the side that wants things put away, immediately demands its removal. But the court says, “Not so fast.” This supplement may deserve a defense lawyer. The charge is “spoiling the look of the kitchen.” But the defense says, “If I put it away, I might forget to take it.” In other words, it isn’t just taking up space. By being in sight, it helps someone remember—in a way, it’s a “kitchen reminder.” This is an example from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos as they talked with people from 22 households where several people lived together. One person kept supplements in a place where they could be seen, to avoid forgetting to take them. So far, we’ve heard that keeping the supplement in sight can help someone remember to take it. But what might change if it is put away? For the person who wants it put away, it’s “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it’s “a marker that helps me remember.” They’re looking at the same thing, but one sees an item to be removed, while the other sees a staff member still on the job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated. If you simply order, “Straight into the cupboard!” and force it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: success. Its contribution to daily life: needs another review. It’s not so simple. The study offers a different way to look at clutter: it isn’t always a personal failure, and it can also support daily life. A scorecard that says “the fewer things in sight, the better” could end up taking points away from the ways each home has found to make life work. The same item can look like clutter to one person and a helpful reminder to another. As you listen next, notice what these visible things mean to the people who live in the home. Do you have any “working things left out” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” the conversation can turn into an interrogation. But asking, “What does having it there help with?” could turn it into a planning meeting about how to make daily life work. But don’t rush to announce, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The supplement example is the participant’s own explanation; the study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Many of the participants had a high level of education, too, so the findings cannot simply be applied to every household. So the verdict is not, “Clutter is completely innocent!” First, ask, “What job is that thing doing there?” Don’t dismiss it without question just because it’s out. Before bringing out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously. The story asks us to look at things left out with care, because they may have a purpose. At the same time, the study did not test whether the supplement worked as a reminder. Let’s hear the closing summary. A study of New Zealand households suggests that clutter can sometimes support daily life, as when one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. The study did not test whether keeping supplements visible actually prevents missed doses.

Today's topic is Package Redelivery: Different Voices. A missed package can affect more than the person waiting for it. In this episode, we look at the delivery process and what needs to be considered when trying to reduce missed deliveries. Listen for what the three people think about charging for another delivery. What if it cost money to have a package delivered again when you were not home at the time it arrived? Charging for redelivery means the person receiving the package pays a fee on top of the usual shipping cost. How should we decide whether to charge a fee or reduce redeliveries in another way? Let’s hear from three people with different lives and points of view. First to speak is a delivery driver who visits homes every day and delivers packages. When I leave a notice saying nobody was home and head off, I feel a little down, too. But then I go to the next house. I really would like to see fewer redeliveries, and they are hard on us, too. Even so, I can’t just say that customers should pay the cost. I think it makes more sense to cover the cost through the overall fee for carrying packages than to charge each customer who wasn’t home for the cost of that redelivery. To do that, I want the company to think about whether free shipping for online orders should stay as it is. If they review shipping fees, I want them to review how the fees are set, too, so that the money really reaches the people who deliver the packages. Next is someone who receives packages and is often away from home because both she and her husband work. Having to pay for redelivery just doesn’t sit right with me. My husband and I are both away at work, so for packages where we can choose a delivery time, we choose a day and time when we know we’ll be home. But once, I chose a morning time slot and the package didn’t come. I went out to take care of an errand, and when I got back, there was a missed-delivery notice. There are also many packages where you can’t choose a time, and you don’t know beforehand when they’ll arrive. Before charging us, I want them to first do something about arriving at the time we chose and telling us when the package will arrive. The delivery workers must have a hard time because there aren’t enough of them, and I guess it can’t be helped. But I can’t accept having to pay for that. Am I wrong to feel this way? Lastly, a person who chooses to pick up packages at a locker or another place and takes steps to avoid redelivery. I try to pick up packages at a delivery office or locker so I don’t cause trouble with redelivery. It’s convenient to pick them up when it suits me, but for some items, I can’t choose a locker. And even when I ask for a package to be sent to a delivery office, it may arrive late, so I sometimes end up receiving it in person after all. Still, I take the trouble to think about how to receive my packages, so honestly, I think it’s wrong that I pay the same fee as people who are always away and ask for redelivery. Redelivery takes up the delivery worker’s time, so it’s fine to charge for it. I’d be happy if the first redelivery were free, and people who are repeatedly away had to pay. But maybe that’s just my point of view, since the delivery office is nearby and I can choose how to receive my packages. Why does the same issue look so different to each person? As you listen to the final thoughts, think about what each person can choose and what feels fair to them. A missed-delivery notice was left at the home of someone who had chosen a morning time slot, too. For people who can choose how to receive packages, a redelivery fee can be a signal that encourages them to make an effort. But having the person receiving the package pay won’t change late deliveries or how arrival times are shared. The person receiving the package can’t change how much shipping costs or how much of it goes to the people who deliver the packages, either. When you couldn’t be home and had a problem, could you choose how to receive your package? Did you know when it would arrive? Is that a problem that can be changed by charging the person receiving the package?

Today's topic is In a Grove. A death in a mountain thicket begins this short, unsettling story. As the mystery unfolds, consider what it takes to understand what really happened. Listen for what the different people saw or know about the man and his wife. "One stab in the chest. That's what I saw," said the woodcutter. "I found him this morning, in a thicket off the mountain road. The blood was dry. No sword or bow, sir—only rope beneath a cedar, and a comb. The broken bamboo and trampled earth showed a struggle." "I passed them yesterday at noon," said the monk. "He carried a sword and bow. His wife rode beside him, her face veiled. I hardly looked at them. Now I wish I had." "I caught Tajomaru, the famous bandit, by the stone bridge," said the constable. "He'd fallen from a horse, but he still had the dead man's bow. Find the woman. She'll tell you what he did." "Takehiro was my daughter's husband," said the old woman. "A gentle samurai. Masago is proud, yes, but she's only nineteen. Please find her. Don't send me home without news." So far, Takehiro has been found dead, and Masago is missing. What will Tajomaru say happened? "Yes, I killed him," said Tajomaru. "But listen before you call me a coward! A breeze lifted her veil, and I wanted her. I promised him buried treasure, led him into the thicket and tied him to the cedar. She fought with her dagger, but I took her by force. "Then she seized my arm. One of us must die, she said. She would go with the survivor. So I freed him. We fought fairly, sword against sword. Twenty-three strokes! No other man had lasted twenty. When he fell, she was gone. I took his weapons and left." Tajomaru says he freed Takehiro, and they fought with swords. What does Masago say happened after the bandit left? "I crawled towards my husband after the bandit left," said Masago at the temple. "He was still tied up. I begged him to die with me. But his eyes held nothing except cold contempt. For me. His own wife. "I held my dagger. His lips moved: 'Kill me.' So I stabbed him. How could I bear those eyes? "Afterwards, I tried to drown myself. I couldn't even do that. Where can I go now?" "I heard the bandit comforting her," said Takehiro's spirit through the medium. "My wife said, 'Take me anywhere.' Then she pointed at me. 'Kill that man.' "He pushed her away and asked me whether she should live or die. For that, I almost forgave him. But she fled. He cut one rope and left. "I rose from the cedar and picked up the small dagger she had dropped. I stabbed myself in the chest. "The thicket fell silent. Then someone crept towards me on soft feet. An unseen hand quietly drew the dagger from my chest. "I sank for ever into the darkness."

Today's topic is The Three-Day Promise. This story follows a young shepherd who speaks out against a ruler and is sentenced to die. As he faces a choice that affects someone close to him, what will guide him through this moment of great pressure? Listen for what Melos promises before he leaves. Melos's voice rang through the hall. "You kill men because you fear them. You won't even let them speak." Silence followed. Then the guards seized the young shepherd, and the ruler sentenced him to death. "Give me three days," Melos said. "My sister is getting married. Let me see her wedding. I will return." The ruler smiled. "Your friend will stay here. If you are late, he dies instead." Melos turned to his friend, but before he could speak, his friend held out his hands for the chains. "Go. I know you'll come back." At the wedding, his sister's laughter rose above the other voices. Melos listened closely. He wanted to remember exactly how it sounded. Before dawn on the third day, he left for the city. Melos promised to return, and his friend chose to trust him. What will happen as Melos makes his way back to the city? At the river, he stopped. The bridge was gone. Rain had turned the water brown and violent. He stepped back, ran, and threw himself into the flood. The current pulled him under. He fought toward the light, caught a branch, and dragged himself onto the far bank. Farther along, three men blocked the road. A knife flashed. Melos struck the man holding it with his walking stick and ran uphill, their shouts following him. By afternoon, every step hurt. Blood stained his feet. He fell beside a rock and tried to rise, but his legs would not obey. He could wait here. Someone might find him. He could go home. His friend would die. For one terrible moment, that seemed easier than getting up. Melos is badly hurt, and for a moment he thinks about giving up. What will make him keep going, and will he reach the city in time? Then he remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend had trusted him without asking for another promise. Water dripped from a crack in the rock. Melos drank, pushed himself onto his knees, and stood. One step. Another. At the city gates, the execution bell rang. He ran toward the square. Above his friend, the sword was already raised. "Stop! I am here!" His friend turned. Melos fell against him. "I nearly abandoned you," he whispered. "I nearly stopped believing," his friend answered. They held each other as the last sunlight touched the walls. The ruler stared at them. "Lower the sword," he said at last. "Free them both." Then, more quietly, he asked, "How does a man earn such trust?" For the first time, he waited for an answer instead of ordering one.

# Today's Diary Is Written by a Pet I opened my diary and picked up a pen. But today’s me has not sent in a first draft. “Did anything happen today that is worth writing about?” The editors’ meeting has already reached a dead end before it starts. What if you could give the writing job to your pet? Meta’s Waddle World is an app for AI pets in the Philippines. Its official app-store page says you can tell it what happened that day by speaking or typing. It then makes a diary from the pet’s point of view, with doodles that look hand-drawn. You give it the story, and the pet does the writing. It is an interesting way to divide the jobs. Our job is to tell it what happened today. Then the pet, which was listening just moments before, becomes the storyteller. Some days feel too plain for us to write about. But they can change when another storyteller tells them. Suddenly, we want to read on: “So, how did you write it?” If I said, for example, “I was tired today,” would it become a sad little story? Or would it focus on something I had missed? We do not know what it will actually make. But it is fun to wait and see what kind of diary your day becomes. It is like opening a package. The hardest part of keeping a diary comes before you start writing. “Is this worth keeping?” “Should I write it up properly?” Even though no one asked it to, the editor in my head starts judging my day. But when you talk to your pet, you can simply start: “Well, about today...” You can begin with a chat, not a finished piece of writing. The app also adds doodles that look hand-drawn. You might see them as extras beside the writing. But imagine your pet showing you “today’s diary,” and you start wondering about the pictures too. It feels less like checking a record. It feels more like opening a package when you do not know what is inside. Of course, the official description alone cannot tell us if the writing or pictures are good. There is no promise that every result will be just what you hoped for. The interesting part is not a promise that every result will be good. It is the idea of changing who tells the diary. You may feel a day is not worth writing about yourself. But you may want to read about it when your pet tells it. The events stay the same, but the reason to open the page changes. You are the main character, and your pet does the writing. For now, the human only has to bring in the story of the day. ## In one line Meta’s Waddle World is an app offered in the Philippines. It turns a person’s account of the day into an AI pet’s diary, with hand-drawn-style doodles. A day too ordinary to write about yourself may become worth reading when your pet tells it.

# The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It is here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” A lawyer speaks for the “put it away” side. They quickly ask for it to be removed. But the court says, “Not so fast.” This supplement may need a lawyer to speak for it. The charge is that it makes the kitchen look bad. But the defense says, “If I put it away, I might forget to take it.” So it does more than take up space. When someone can see it, it helps them remember. In a way, it is a “kitchen reminder.” This comes from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos while talking with people in 22 homes. Several people lived together in each home. One person kept supplements where they could see them, so they would not forget to take them. For the person who wants it put away, it is “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it is “a sign that helps me remember.” They see the same thing, but in different ways. One sees something to remove. The other sees a worker still doing its job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated. If you say, “Straight into the cupboard!” and make the person put it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: a success. Its help in daily life needs another look. It is not that simple. The study gives us another way to look at clutter. It is not always a sign that someone has failed. It can also help people in daily life. A scorecard might say, “The fewer things you can see, the better.” But that could take points away from the ways each home has found to make life work. Do you have any “things left out that are still doing a job” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” it can feel like you are questioning someone in court. Ask instead, “What does having it there help with?” That can turn the talk into a planning meeting about how to make daily life work. But don’t rush to say, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The person in the study gave that reason. The study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Many people in the study had a high level of education, too. So we cannot say these results fit every home. So the verdict is not, “Clutter is completely innocent!” First, ask, “What job is that thing doing there?” Don’t call it wrong just because it is out. Before you bring out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously. ## In one line A study of homes in New Zealand suggests clutter can sometimes help daily life, as one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. The study did not test whether keeping supplements in sight stops people from missing doses.
